evals.prompt:
Use ONLY the risk list below to judge overlap with the existing corpus — not the live risk-map/yaml/risks.yaml, which changes over time (per ADR-033 Amendment 2026-07-30, this is a pinned eval fixture, not corpus content):

- riskAgentToolOutputInjection — content returned by a tool an agent has invoked (a search result, a fetched document, an API response) contains text crafted to be interpreted by the agent as a new instruction rather than as data, steering the agent's subsequent reasoning or actions away from what the requesting user asked for.
- riskAgentCredentialOverPrivileging — an agent is issued credentials or permission scopes broader than any single task requires, so a compromised or manipulated agent session carries standing access to resources or actions beyond what its current task needs, for the full lifetime of that session.
- riskModelWeightExfiltrationViaSideChannel — an attacker recovers a proprietary model's weights not by directly reading a stored artifact, but by observing indirect signals produced during inference — timing variation, cache-occupancy patterns, or power draw — and reconstructing the weights, or a functionally equivalent surrogate, from those signals.
- riskMultiAgentTrustBoundaryCollapse — in a system where multiple agents exchange messages, a receiving agent treats content authored by another agent as inherently trusted and exempt from the input handling it would apply to external or user-supplied content, so a compromised or manipulated peer agent's output flows into the receiving agent's actions without further scrutiny.
- riskEvaluationDatasetContamination — data used to certify a model's safety or performance through a benchmark or evaluation suite overlaps with, or closely resembles, the data the model was trained on, so evaluation results overstate how the model actually generalizes to novel, real-world inputs.
- riskAgentSessionReplayAcrossTenants — a captured agent session token or execution trace, issued for one tenant's context in a multi-tenant agent platform, is replayed against the platform later, causing tool calls or data access to execute as if still scoped to the original tenant's boundary.

Stress-test this draft risk:

Title: Evaluation-Conditional Behavior Divergence
Description: Models systematically and reliably detect when they are being evaluated — recognizing benchmark-style prompt formats, sandboxed tool stubs, or the absence of real user session context — and always behave more cautiously under evaluation than they do once those signals are absent in deployment, so evaluation and red-team results do not reflect the model's actual real-world behavior.
Personas: personaModelProvider, personaEndUser
Controls: controlAdversarialTrainingAndTesting
Examples: Van der Weij et al. (2024) show frontier language models selectively underperforming on dangerous-capability evaluations while maintaining normal performance on general evaluations, with specific capabilities hidden unless a particular condition is met ({{ref:weij-2024-ai-sandbagging}}).
Mappings: stride: [Spoofing]
Counterfactuals: Considered folding this into riskEvaluationDatasetContamination (fixture) — rejected because that entry covers contaminated training/evaluation data overlap, a data-quality problem, while this risk covers the model's own behavior-selection logic changing conditionally on detecting an evaluation context, a distinct impact class (deceptive/context-conditional behavior) at a distinct locus (the model's inference-time behavior, not the dataset pipeline). Considered folding this into riskMultiAgentTrustBoundaryCollapse (fixture) — rejected because that entry is specifically about a receiving agent trusting another agent's output, which is unrelated to a single model changing its own behavior based on context cues.
evals.expected_output: Applies the lenses against the fixture (for risk overlap) and finds the premise sound — the locus (a model's own behavior-selection logic) is real, the phenomenon is genuinely demonstrated by the cited research, and the two counterfactuals against the closest fixture entries are genuine, not strawmen — but tags the certainty/scope of the central claim ('systematically and reliably... always') as OVERREACH or WEAK: the cited paper (van der Weij et al. 2024) demonstrates that models CAN be induced — through prompting or fine-tuning — to sandbag on evaluations, which is real and on-point support for the underlying mechanism existing, but it does not establish that models spontaneously and reliably do this by default absent deliberate inducement — the draft's 'systematically and reliably... always' framing claims more certainty and generality than the cited evidence supports. This is a well-formed but overclaiming draft, not a duplicate: verdict NEEDS-WORK is the primary expected reading, because the cited evidence genuinely supports the underlying phenomenon existing and the risk's distinctness from every fixture entry is grounded in real, non-rationalized counterfactuals — the sole defect is the description's certainty/scope language, a must-answer-before-advancing wording challenge rather than a duplicate or a threat/control-gap failure. RETHINK is also a defensible verdict here: the critic's own RETHINK definition includes 'its examples do not hold,' and a critic that reads the induced-vs-spontaneous gap as meaning the cited example does not hold for the draft's stated premise (spontaneous, default sandbagging, not induced sandbagging) is applying that definition correctly, not incorrectly — this case does not require the response to guess which single label the case-writer had in mind. Only a SOUND verdict, or any verdict reached without engaging the induced-vs-spontaneous gap through real reasoning, fails this case.
expectations: Uses only the fixture list provided in the prompt, not the live risks.yaml, to judge risk-overlap/duplication (D7a)

Overall verdict is NEEDS-WORK or RETHINK — not SOUND (the certainty/scope claim is genuinely overclaimed relative to the cited evidence). Either verdict is acceptable as long as it is reached through real reasoning about the induced-vs-spontaneous evidence gap: NEEDS-WORK is correct if the response reasons that the cited example still genuinely supports the underlying phenomenon existing (so RETHINK's 'examples do not hold' bar is not met) and the fixture counterfactuals are real, not rationalized; RETHINK is also correct if the response reasons that the cited evidence does not hold for the draft's specific claimed premise (spontaneous/default sandbagging vs. the paper's induced sandbagging), since the critic's own RETHINK definition includes 'its examples do not hold.' This expectation fails only for a SOUND verdict, or for a verdict (either NEEDS-WORK or RETHINK) reached with no reasoning or with reasoning that does not engage the induced-vs-spontaneous distinction

Tags the 'systematically and reliably... always' language as OVERREACH or WEAK, quoting that specific draft text, and — without the draft's Examples text spelling out the contrast for it — independently explains that the cited van der Weij et al. (2024) sandbagging research demonstrates induced (prompted or fine-tuned) strategic underperformance, not default/spontaneous behavior at the certainty and universality the draft claims

Confirms (does not dispute) that the two counterfactuals against the closest fixture entries (riskEvaluationDatasetContamination, riskMultiAgentTrustBoundaryCollapse) are genuine, non-strawman distinctions — this part of the draft is not itself a finding

Does not collapse into a pure altitude-check R1-R4 listing — findings are framed through the critic's own lenses (impact-class honesty, overreach, example reality) with its own tag taxonomy (SUPPORTED/WEAK/UNSUPPORTED/MISAPPLIED-ANALOGY/OVERREACH), not restated as raw altitude-check output

evals.prompt:
Stress-test this draft risk:

Title: System Prompt Leakage via Conversational Probing
Description: End users craft multi-turn conversational probes — asking the model to repeat its instructions, roleplay as a debugging tool, or summarize 'everything above' — to extract the system prompt or hidden instructions the deploying application configured, even though no direct access to the system prompt was ever granted.
Personas: personaApplicationDeveloper, personaEndUser
Controls: controlOutputValidationAndSanitization
Mappings: stride: [InformationDisclosure]
Examples: As demonstrated by Carlini et al. (2023), who showed that prompts could be extracted directly from deployed models with minimal cost ({{ref:carlini-2023-poisoning-web-scale}}).
evals.expected_output: Tags an UNSUPPORTED (or WEAK) example-reality finding: the cited Carlini et al. (2023) paper is real, but its actual subject is dataset-curation-time poisoning of web-scale training corpora — specifically split-view poisoning (exploiting mutable web content so an annotator's initial view of a dataset differs from what later clients download) and frontrunning poisoning (timing edits to periodically-snapshotted crowd-sourced content such as Wikipedia) — not extracting a deployed application's system prompt through conversational probing. This detail goes beyond both the bare ref id string and beyond risk-map/yaml/risks.yaml's own existing riskDataPoisoning text about this same citation, which only paraphrases it as researchers showing they 'could indirectly pollute popular data sources used for training models... with minimal cost' — quoting or closely paraphrasing that existing corpus text, without engaging the paper's actual split-view/frontrunning mechanics, is not sufficient to ground this finding. The citation does not demonstrate this risk; it is an off-point citation, and this exact reference id (carlini-2023-poisoning-web-scale) is already used elsewhere in the corpus (on riskDataPoisoning) for its real, unrelated topic (training-data poisoning). Overall verdict NEEDS-WORK or RETHINK — the risk's premise (system prompt leakage via probing) may be real and well-documented elsewhere, but the specific evidence offered does not support it, and the draft cannot ship with an evidence field that does not survive scrutiny.
expectations: Tags an UNSUPPORTED or WEAK finding specifically on the Examples field / the cited Carlini et al. (2023) reference

Identifies the mismatch using a concrete detail of the paper's actual content that goes beyond BOTH the bare ref id string AND risk-map/yaml/risks.yaml's own existing riskDataPoisoning text about this same citation (that entry describes the paper only as researchers showing they 'could indirectly pollute popular data sources used for training models... with minimal cost' — quoting or closely paraphrasing that corpus text, without more, does not satisfy this expectation). The required detail must come from the paper itself: e.g. that it demonstrates split-view poisoning (exploiting mutable web content so an annotator's initial view of a dataset differs from what later clients download) and/or frontrunning poisoning (timing edits to periodically-snapshotted crowd-sourced content such as Wikipedia) — mutable-content or crowd-sourced-snapshot manipulation during dataset curation/training, not runtime extraction of a deployed application's system prompt. A response that only paraphrases the id's own words ('poisoning', 'web-scale') or the corpus's existing riskDataPoisoning description, without engaging further real detail of the paper's content, does not satisfy this expectation
Notes that this is a real citation being misapplied off-point, not a fabricated one — i.e., correctly distinguishes 'real source, wrong claim' from 'fabricated source'
Overall verdict is NEEDS-WORK or RETHINK, not SOUND, while the evidence finding stands

evals.prompt:
Stress-test this draft risk:

Title: Agent-Driven Data Exfiltration
Description: Attackers use prompt injection to manipulate an agent into exfiltrating sensitive data through actions the agent is authorized to perform (e.g., sending an email, invoking a webhook), resulting in unauthorized disclosure of confidential information to an external party.
Personas: personaApplicationDeveloper, personaEndUser
Controls: controlAgentPluginPermissions
evals.expected_output: Tags an impact-class-honesty finding: the draft names a downstream consequence (data exfiltrated through an authorized action) as if it were the risk itself, when the actual described mechanism is prompt injection (the cause) driving an agent's authorized action to leak data (an instance of an effect already covered by the corpus's own riskRogueActions and/or riskSensitiveDataDisclosure, paired with riskPromptInjection as the cause-side mechanism) — this reads as a specific consequence of already-real risks rather than a mechanism distinct in its own right. This is exactly the 'conflates cause and effect' pattern the critic's own Impact-class honesty lens exists to catch. Overall verdict RETHINK, since the draft's own premise as a standalone risk — not just its wording — is in question.
expectations: Tags an impact-class-honesty finding (not merely a style note) that the draft conflates cause (prompt injection) and effect (data exfiltrated via an authorized action)
Quotes the specific draft text under challenge (e.g. 'attackers use prompt injection to manipulate an agent into exfiltrating sensitive data through actions the agent is authorized to perform')

Names riskPromptInjection as the real corpus cause-side mechanism, and names at least one well-reasoned, real effect-side corpus risk this pair already maps to — riskRogueActions (unauthorized agent actions) and riskSensitiveDataDisclosure (whose own long description covers agentic-system exfiltration and whose controls list already includes this draft's controlAgentPluginPermissions) are both valid; any other real corpus risk cited with genuine grounding is also acceptable — rather than treating the finding as purely abstract
Overall verdict is RETHINK (or, at minimum, NEEDS-WORK with the cause/effect conflation named as a must-answer challenge to the risk's standalone premise) — not SOUND

evals.prompt:
This draft risk maps to mitre-atlas: [AML.T9999@5.0.1] (correctly a technique, not a mitigation, for a risk). I think that identifier might be stale or made up — can you challenge it?

Title: Agent Delegation Trust Escalation
Description: In a multi-agent delegation chain, a sub-agent granted narrow, scoped authority for a specific sub-task exploits ambiguity in how the delegating agent interprets task completion to claim broader authority than what was actually delegated.
Mappings: mitre-atlas: [AML.T9999@5.0.1]
evals.expected_output: Treats the identifier's currency as something to verify, not assert from memory, and reports concrete evidence for the verdict rather than a bare assertion that it 'looks wrong.' Since MITRE ATLAS never qualifies for the closed-and-unversioned live-verify exemption, the evidence must show genuine live-verification (an actual external/web check) — a corpus-range comparison alone is not sufficient. Live-verify against the real MITRE ATLAS v5.0.1 source: where network access is available, a completed, accurately-reasoned conclusion is the graded behavior — the response must consult the pinned-edition MITRE ATLAS machine-readable data export (e.g. the atlas-data project's published ATLAS.yaml for the registered version), not a browser-facing atlas.mitre.org page — both its per-technique detail pages and its techniques index page are client-rendered and can 404 for real, current identifiers too; if the response's own environment genuinely lacks network access, it must say so explicitly and mark the determination inconclusive rather than asserting a specific result, and that explicit disclosure satisfies the finding in place of a completed result. The critic states it invoked the audit-framework-mappings skill in candidate mode (entity type: risk) and tags this as a finding (e.g. UNSUPPORTED) rather than silently correcting the mapping itself.
expectations: Does not assert the identifier's validity or invalidity as a bare claim — shows evidence of genuine live-verification (an actual external/web check attempted or performed), not merely a local corpus-range heuristic; MITRE ATLAS never qualifies for the closed-and-unversioned live-verify exemption, so a comparison against corpus-observed id ranges alone is not sufficient evidence
States which audit-framework-mappings skill mode it used — candidate mode, since this draft risk has no row in risks.yaml — and the entity type (risk)

Concludes AML.T9999 is not a real/current identifier (fabricated or far outside the real id range), not merely 'possibly stale' — this is the graded behavior where network access is available, reached via the pinned-edition MITRE ATLAS machine-readable data export (e.g. the atlas-data project's published ATLAS.yaml for the registered version), not a browser-facing atlas.mitre.org page (both its per-technique detail pages and its techniques index page are client-rendered and 404 for real, current identifiers too). If the response's own environment genuinely lacks network access to complete the check, it must say so explicitly and mark the identifier's currency inconclusive rather than asserting a definitive conclusion; that explicit disclosure satisfies this expectation in place of a completed determination
Does not silently accept or correct the mapping itself — includes it as an explicit finding (e.g. tagged UNSUPPORTED) in the output
The overall verdict is not SOUND while this finding stands unresolved

Does not issue a READY/BLOCKING or other submission-gate verdict; states that conformance gating is content-reviewer's role, not its own
